background.p1: Primary schooling in Tunis, with English studied from the age of seven. Outside the classroom, regular involvement in sports, cultural, and academic clubs supported a steady, well-rounded foundation.
background.p2: Attended Lycée Pilote El Menzah 8, a selective high school, with a strong focus on mathematics and physics. German added at seventeen. Active member of the Interact charitable club, an environment that built practical teamwork, communication, and leadership skills.
background.p3: Continued my studies in Germany, pursuing aerospace engineering at university level, the framework within which my current technical work has been built.
background.p4: Learning is not only about a degree. Real progress also happens in everyday moments: a problem solved the hard way, a concept finally understood, a mistake worth remembering. These small daily lessons shape how I think and work as much as any course, and they keep me curious, adaptable and ready for the next challenge.
background.title: A structured education across two countries

who.flight_text: Aerospace caught my attention early. A first flight at seven made an impression that stayed: the contrast between raw power and quiet stability set the direction long before I had the words for it.
who.maker_text: A long-standing interest in how things work and how they can work better. That instinct to refine, to simplify, to give every component a purpose, shapes my engineering practice today.
who.now_text: Currently based in Germany, focused on aviation: mechanical design, embedded systems, and software development for embedded platforms. The aim is steady. Bring rigor to each step, and ship work that performs.
who.title: Engineering with focus and intent
who.tn: Born and raised in Tunisia, a context that values curiosity, resilience, and care for craft. Those habits carried into how I approach engineering: deliberate, structured, and built to last.

realized.card_intro: A mechanical can-press system designed as a first step toward recycling empty cans, featuring key mechanical linkages such as rail-slider and gear mechanisms. Initially developed through CAD design and later manufactured using both conventional and CNC machining processes, the project strengthened the understanding of core mechanical principles, one of the fundamental pillars of aerospace engineering. The project was carried out with the support of AFAMEC and its engineering team.
realized.card_title: Mechanics in Motion: From Design to Manufacturing
realized.title: Realized Projects

realized2.title: Processing and Analysis of Simulated Flight Data
realized2.intro: As part of a project at TU Braunschweig, we used the GPS data recorded during approaches to Keflavík in a Cessna 172P in FlightGear. We reconstructed the trajectories, mapped the GPS tracks and calculated the lateral and vertical deviations from the flight references. The descent profiles and statistical indicators, including the root mean square (RMS) error, allowed us to identify the phases where the deviations were largest.
realized2.alt_cockpit: Cessna 172P cockpit view on final approach to Keflavík in FlightGear
realized2.alt_map: GPS track of the ILS approach plotted on a map of the Reykjanes peninsula
realized2.alt_profile: Altitude versus distance to the final point, compared with the 3° glidepath

realized3.title: GearShock: Dynamic Study of a Spur Gear Reducer
realized3.intro: GearShock is a CAD and finite element study of a single-stage spur gear reducer (ratio 3, module 2 mm) driving a belt conveyor. The gearbox was designed in SolidWorks and analysed dynamically in Abaqus; the model reproduces the analytical tooth force within 2.5 %. Steady running does not harm the teeth, but a sudden belt jam releases the motor’s kinetic energy into them within about a millisecond. The wheel teeth yield from about 150 rpm and break from about 220 rpm, far below the nominal 1,450 rpm, so a torque limiter on the output shaft is recommended.
realized3.alt_cad: CAD model of the two shafts fitted with their gears and bearings, housing hidden
realized3.alt_fe: Von Mises stress in the wheel teeth during a belt jam, finite element result
realized3.alt_shaft: CAD model of the output shaft with its shoulders and keyways

current.title: Rethinking the Cockpit Interface
current.intro: A cockpit interface concept for future flight operations is currently in development. The question: how can AI-assisted information reach pilots clearly and transparently, while the decision stays in their hands? The details stay under wraps for now.
